t: Longest Increasing Subsequence II — Segment Tree over DP Values
o: We need the longest strictly increasing subsequence where each adjacent pair differs by at most k. The natural DP is: `dp[i]` = length of the longest valid subsequence ending at index i, computed as `1 + max(dp[j])` over all earlier j with `nums[i] - k <= nums[j] < nums[i]`. A brute force over all pairs is O(n^2), too slow for n = 10^5. Since values are bounded by 10^5, we can reindex the DP by *value* instead of index and use a range-max query structure (segment tree) to answer 'best dp among values in [v-k, v-1]' in O(log V). Coordinate compression isn't even needed since values fit in a fixed range. Example 1: processing values 4,2,1,4,3,4,5,8,15 with k=3 builds dp [1,1,1,2,2,3,4,5,5], answer 5. Constraints (n, values up to 1e5) point directly at an O(n log V) segment tree solution.
k: dp[i] depends only on max dp among previous elements whose value lies in [nums[i]-k, nums[i]-1] — a range maximum query.
Indexing the segment tree by value (not position) turns the O(n) scan into an O(log V) query.
Strictly increasing means query range is [v-k, v-1]; update at value v uses dp+1.

a.i: For each element, scan all previous elements and take the best dp among those that can precede it (value in [v-k, v-1]). This directly implements the recurrence but is quadratic — fine for understanding, too slow for n = 10^5.
s: Initialize dp array of all ones.
For each i, loop j < i; if nums[i]-k <= nums[j] < nums[i], set dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j]+1).
a.t: O(n^2) — nested loops over all pairs.

a.i: Build a max segment tree of size M = max(nums) + 1 indexed by value. For each number v in order, query the max dp over values [max(1, v-k), v-1], set cur = query + 1, then point-update position v to cur. Each operation is O(log M), giving O(n log M) total. This works because when processing left to right, the tree contains exactly the dp values of all previously seen elements, keyed by their value.
s: Let M = max(nums); build a max segment tree of size M initialized to 0.
For each v in nums: lo = max(1, v-k), hi = v-1.
If hi >= lo, cur = rangeMax(lo, hi) + 1, else cur = 1.
Point-update position v with cur; track global answer.
a.t: O(n log M) where M is the max value — one query and one update per element, each O(log M).

w: In an interview, start from the O(n^2) DP, then observe the range-max structure and pivot to a segment tree keyed by value. Pitfalls: forgetting strictness (query upper bound must be v-1, not v), forgetting to clamp lo at 1 (values are positive so v-k could be <= 0), and off-by-one errors in iterative segment tree bounds. Edge cases: single element returns 1; all equal elements return 1; k larger than any gap behaves like classic LIS. Follow-ups: handle negative values or huge ranges via coordinate compression, or stream/online variants where a BIT with binary-searched prefix max also works.
